record.administering_agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services (County Executive Office)
record.typical_award_size: Gap loans historically $500,000 to $2,000,000 per project: $2,000,000 requested for Burbank Housing Stoddard West (51 units, 2017), $650,000 plus $148,000 for Turley Flats in St. Helena (8 units, 2017-2018), $500,000 for SAHA Manzanita Family Apartments (51 units, 2019, with $750,000 HEAP), $200,000 for 963 Pope Street in St. Helena (5 units, 2025). The 2010 NOFA offered $5,000,000 plus $2,000,000 reserved for farmworker housing. By 2017 the fund had loaned $22,000,000 for more than 1,000 units since 1992; fee revenue runs about $2,000,000 a year and the fund also pays for farmworker centers, homeless services and fair housing.
record.per_unit_cap: No fixed cap. The joint City and County Multi Family Transaction Underwriting Guidelines (Jan 21, 2020) size the subsidy by gap analysis against comparable projects; developer fee for small projects capped at $25,000 per unit for units 1-10, $15,000 for units 11-30, $12,000 above 30.
record.affordability_requirement: 55-year affordability covenant for rental projects (40 years for County-assisted ownership). County preference for projects in the unincorporated area, deeper affordability, permanent affordability and local workers where allowed by law. Loans may be forgiven after 40 to 55 years by Board action.
record.next_deadline: Rolling since the 2010 NOFA; the County accepts applications year-round under the 2010 application and the 2020 joint underwriting guidelines. Requests go to the Napa County Housing Commission and then the Board of Supervisors; time them to the CTCAC round.
record.layering_notes: Capitalized by residential inclusionary in-lieu and impact fees and nonresidential housing impact fees under County Code Chapter 18.107 (Ordinance 1026, 1992); the October 21, 2025 fee overhaul (phased in from Jan 16, 2026) should raise annual revenue. Terms per the joint guidelines: 3.0% simple interest (lower if needed for feasibility), 55-year term from permanent loan conversion, 50/50 split of residual receipts between the City/County and developer, balance due at maturity, subordinate to senior debt, 90% maximum LTV on senior debt, monitoring fee $100 per unit for the first 40 units. Deferred developer fee may be repaid from cash flow within 15 years before residual receipts split. Most funded projects are inside the cities; the County obtains RHNA transfer credits in exchange (80% of County RHNA goes to the City of Napa under the Napa Pipe agreement through 2058), which limits funds for other jurisdictions. County loan is public money, so state prevailing wage applies under Labor Code 1720 unless an exemption fits. napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the program page is https://www.napacounty.gov/443/Affordable-Housing-Projects and the source given is the joint underwriting guidelines hosted by the City of Napa.

record.program_name: Affordable Housing Impact Fee and Inclusionary Requirements (County Code Chapter 18.107)
record.administering_agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services; Planning, Building and Environmental Services
record.typical_award_size: Not a subsidy; it capitalizes the Affordable Housing Fund. Fees adopted Oct 21, 2025 (3-2 vote), effective Jan 16, 2026, phased 50% in 2026, 75% in 2027, 100% in 2028: residential per sq ft $0 up to 2,500 sq ft, $43 for 2,501-3,500 sq ft (was $10.75), $86 above 3,500 sq ft (was $12.25); ADUs under 751 sq ft exempt. Nonresidential per sq ft: hotel $100 (was $9), retail and restaurant $58.40 (was $7.50), office $14.68 (was $5.25), industrial $7.70 (was $4.50), warehouse $7.50 (was $3.60).
record.affordability_requirement: Ownership projects: 20% of single-family detached units or 17% of attached units for moderate income (120% AMI) households, 40-year restrictions. Rental projects pay housing fees or elect the alternative of 12% of units at low income rents under a rent regulatory agreement. Exempt: farmworker units of 1,200 sq ft or less, 100% affordable projects, certain multifamily and SRO projects, projects of four or fewer units may pay a per-unit fee. Equivalency proposals (off-site units, land dedication) allowed with Planning Commission approval.
record.next_deadline: Fees apply to applications filed after Jan 15, 2026 at 50% of the new schedule; 75% in 2027; full schedule in 2028. The Board also directed staff to create a fee deferral program for owners who rent units as affordable housing; terms not yet published.
record.layering_notes: Relevant to developers two ways: 100% affordable multifamily is exempt from the fee, and the fee stream funds the County Affordable Housing Fund. A fee exemption or waiver can count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), so confirm prevailing wage exposure with counsel. Applies only in unincorporated Napa County; each city has its own inclusionary and linkage rules (Pass 3). Code text was read from the Zoneomics mirror (Ordinances 1334 of 2010, 1386 of 2013, 1491 of June 4, 2024 and 1495 of Sept 24, 2024); fee amounts come from Sonoma Index-Tribune and CBS Bay Area coverage of the Oct 21, 2025 vote. napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the official FAQ is https://www.napacounty.gov/3951/Affordable-Housing-Impact-Fee-Housing-Co.

record.program_name: Napa County Density Bonus and Incentives (County Code 18.107.170-18.107.190)
record.administering_agency: Napa County Planning, Building and Environmental Services
record.typical_award_size: Density bonus, incentives and concessions, parking reductions and development standard waivers per Government Code 65915; the chapter defers to state law where they conflict.
record.affordability_requirement: State density bonus thresholds; County requires 55-year affordability for rental bonus units and 45 years for for-sale units. Requests must be filed with the first discretionary permit with detailed submittals; denial of incentives or waivers requires specified written findings.
record.layering_notes: Unincorporated Napa County is mostly Agricultural Preserve and Agricultural Watershed zoning, so multifamily sites are scarce; the 2023-2031 Housing Element (adopted Dec 19, 2023, HCD compliance letter Feb 22, 2024) relies on a 106-unit RHNA and RHNA transfers to the City of Napa. Inclusionary units count toward the state bonus (Latinos Unidos del Valle de Napa y Solano v. County of Napa, 2013). Ordinance 1495 (Sept 24, 2024) updated the incentives and density bonus sections. Code text read from the Zoneomics mirror; napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; confirm against the official code at library.municode.com or the County.

record.program_name: Affordable Unit Permit Fee Waiver and Expedited Processing (County Code 18.107.120)
record.administering_agency: Napa County Planning, Building and Environmental Services
record.typical_award_size: Building permit application fee waivers for compliant affordable units, flexibility in unit size and finishes, attached units allowed in single-family projects, and expedited processing. Housing impact fees are also refundable if a project does not proceed and a refund is requested within 90 days.
record.affordability_requirement: Units must satisfy Chapter 18.107 affordability (40-year minimum; 55 years for density bonus rentals).
record.next_deadline: The Oct 21, 2025 fee action also directed staff to design a fee deferral program for owners renting units as affordable housing; watch for the ordinance in 2026.
record.layering_notes: Modest value for multifamily since the chapter is written around inclusionary units in small unincorporated projects. Waived fees count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4) and can trigger state prevailing wage, so confirm with counsel. Code text read from the Zoneomics mirror; napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; confirm with the County.

record.program_name: HOME and CDBG, Napa County (state non-entitlement status)
record.administering_agency: California HCD state HOME and CDBG programs; Napa County Housing and Community Services as applicant
record.typical_award_size: None directly. Napa County is not a HUD CDBG entitlement urban county or a HOME participating jurisdiction. The City of Napa is the only CDBG entitlement in the county (FY 2024-25 entitlement $583,519) and draws HOME and ESG through State HCD grants. No County of Napa state HOME or CDBG award for 2024 or 2025 surfaced in HCD award lists.
record.per_unit_cap: HOME per-unit subsidy limits (24 CFR 92.250) apply to any state HOME award.
record.affordability_requirement: State HOME: 20% of HOME units at 50% AMI, rest at 60% AMI, 55-year HCD covenant. State CDBG: 51% of units for households at or below 80% AMI.
record.next_deadline: Follow HCD state HOME and CDBG NOFAs (state records). A developer in unincorporated Napa or the four small cities needs the County or city to apply as the state HOME or CDBG grantee.
record.layering_notes: There is no county-level HOME or CDBG pipeline to layer in Napa; this is a negative finding. The City of Napa CDBG and HOME programs are Pass 3. Napa County received $207,965 of State ESG for CA-517 in the 2024 NOFA, usable for shelter and rapid rehousing, not capital. HOME and CDBG carry federal Davis-Bacon (CDBG at 8+ units, HOME at 12+ units) and state prevailing wage. Status inferred from the City of Napa 2025-2030 Consolidated Plan, the City FY 2024-25 CAPER and HCD award lists; confirm with the County.

record.program_name: Napa County Housing Authority Farmworker Centers (CSA No. 4 assessment and HCD matching funds)
record.administering_agency: Napa County Housing Authority (Board of Supervisors sitting as the Authority)
record.typical_award_size: Operating support for three county-owned dormitory centers (180 beds, about 400 farmworkers a year): County Service Area No. 4 vineyard assessment at $14 per planted acre raises about $650,000 a year (about 30% of operating cost); HCD Napa County Farmworker Centers Account match up to $250,000 a year (Health and Safety Code 50711.5, funded by SB 2); AB 1890 (Chapter 905, Statutes of 2026, signed Sept 30, 2026) raises the match to $500,000 a year once the Legislature appropriates it; AB 317 (2017) $200,000 General Fund support expires FY 2028-29. The County Affordable Housing Fund also subsidizes operations.
record.affordability_requirement: Centers serve migrant and seasonal farmworkers; AB 1890 bars use of the state funds to house H-2A workers.
record.next_deadline: Not available to outside developers; funds flow only to the County-owned centers. CSA 4 assessment is reauthorized by growers every five years.
record.layering_notes: Negative finding for private sponsors: Napa's only county housing authority is a farmworker-center operator with no Housing Choice Vouchers or development lending; the public housing agency for the county is the Housing Authority of the City of Napa. Farmworker rental projects in Napa instead layer the state Joe Serna Jr. Farmworker Housing Grant, the State Farmworker Housing Tax Credit (Pass 1) and the County Affordable Housing Fund, which once reserved $2,000,000 for farmworker projects and whose fees exempt farmworker units of 1,200 sq ft or less. The 2024 Napa County Farmworker Housing Needs and Impacts Assessment found 16% of year-round and 26% of seasonal workers in overcrowded housing. napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the Authority page is https://www.napacounty.gov/467/Housing-Authority (707-253-4112).

record.program_name: Napa County Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) housing interventions
record.administering_agency: Napa County Health and Human Services Agency, Behavioral Health Division
record.typical_award_size: Unknown. Under Proposition 1, 30% of each county's BHSA allocation must fund housing interventions beginning FY 2026-27, with up to 25% of that for capital; counties under 200,000 population (Napa qualifies) may request exemptions from the housing requirements in the FY 2026-29 Integrated Plan. Napa's draft Integrated Plan (FY 2026-27 through 2028-29) was out for comment April 1 to May 1, 2026 with a Behavioral Health Board hearing May 13, 2026; whether Napa requested the exemption or budgeted capital is not confirmed.
record.affordability_requirement: Housing interventions serve people with serious mental illness or substance use disorder who are homeless or at risk, with half of housing funds for chronically homeless individuals unless exempted.
record.next_deadline: Integrated Plan took effect July 1, 2026; annual updates follow. Ask Napa HHSA Behavioral Health whether capital or operating subsidies will be offered to PSH sponsors.
record.layering_notes: Napa's small BHSA allocation makes operating subsidies or rental assistance for a handful of PSH units the realistic ask; pair with Homekey+ or HHAP. Public funds, so capital triggers prevailing wage. No Napa-specific document could be opened: napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the BHSA page is https://www.napacounty.gov/338 and the Integrated Plan Executive Summary is DocumentCenter/View/41683. Facts above come from the DHCS BHSA policy manual and Integrated Plan template plus search excerpts.

record.program_name: Napa County Affordable ADU Forgivable Loan Program (single-unit, recorded for completeness)
record.administering_agency: Napa County Housing and Community Services
record.typical_award_size: Forgivable construction loans of $45,000 to $105,000 per ADU (by bedroom count and design) for homeowners in Napa County; launched March 2023, updated underwriting guidelines adopted March 10, 2026, information session April 30, 2026. Funded from the Affordable Housing Fund (piloted with $100,000 in 2017).
record.affordability_requirement: ADU rented to a household at or below 80% AMI for at least five years; loan forgiven on compliance, otherwise repayable.
record.next_deadline: Open until funds are exhausted; applications through the County.
record.layering_notes: Not a multifamily source; recorded so the Affordable Housing Fund's competing uses are visible (ADU loans, farmworker centers, homeless services and fair housing all draw on the same fee revenue). Terms from the Napa Valley Community Foundation launch notice (March 17, 2023) and County news releases quoted in search results; napacounty.gov pages and DocumentCenter PDFs sit behind Cloudflare and refused automated access on 2026-11-06, so the county's own page could not be opened; the 2026 notice is https://www.napacounty.gov/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=858.

record.program_name: Napa fee deferral and reduced building permit fees for affordable and workforce housing (Housing Element Programs H2-2.8 and H2-1.1)
record.administering_agency: City of Napa Community Development Department (Building Division) and Housing Division
record.typical_award_size: Documented practice of deferring impact fees to occupancy for any qualifying affordable project (Prohousing matrix item 3C; Housing Element constraint analysis). Housing Element Program H2-2.8 commits to fees deferred, reduced or waived plus fast tracking for 100% affordable projects by 2025 (reported as not initiated in the 2023 APR). Napa Valley Register coverage of a 2021 council vote (3-2) reports a 50% reduction in building permit, plan check and inspection fees for housing at or below 120% AMI and for ADUs of 500 square feet or less; that fee resolution was not located on cityofnapa.org this pass.
record.per_unit_cap: Not applicable; percentage reduction of permit fees, no dollar cap published.
record.affordability_requirement: Affordable and workforce housing at or below 120% AMI per the reported 2021 action; impact fee deferral applies to affordable units as defined in NMC 15.94 (80% AMI or below).
record.next_deadline: Applied at permit issuance on request. Confirm the current master fee schedule discount and the status of the H2-2.8 fast track program with the Building Division (NapaON permit portal) before underwriting; Housing Element fee realignment is due by 2028.
record.layering_notes: Fee relief is modest relative to the impact fee and TOT loans but is routinely combined with them. Napa Valley Unified School District and Napa Sanitation District fees are outside the City's control. Waived or reduced fees can count as public funds under Labor Code 1720(b)(4), so confirm with counsel. The Prohousing matrix (source_url) and the Housing Element were opened; the 50% figure comes from news coverage and is marked needs_confirmation.

record.program_name: Napa Successor Agency housing funds: 20% Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund (Fund 229) and Local Housing Fund (Fund 230)
record.administering_agency: Housing Authority of the City of Napa as housing successor to the Napa Community Redevelopment Agency; City Housing Division staff
record.typical_award_size: Residual redevelopment housing assets (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund under Health and Safety Code 34176) administered by the Housing Authority, plus a Local Housing Fund. The Prohousing matrix (item 4H) states the City created the Low/Mod Fund from residual redevelopment funds and uses it for affordable housing. Current balances were not found online this pass; the AB 987 database of RDA assisted units is posted at cityofnapa.org/DocumentCenter/View/101.
record.affordability_requirement: Health and Safety Code 34176.1 rules for housing successors: funds for households at or below 80% AMI with at least 30% of expenditures for 30% AMI households over each five year period, 55-year rental covenants.
record.next_deadline: No separate NOFA; deployed through the Housing Authority Board (the City Council plus two resident commissioners) with the rolling impact fee and TOT NOFA. Confirm balances with the Housing Division (707-257-9543) and the latest SB 341 housing successor annual report.
record.layering_notes: Likely small relative to the impact fee ($8.7 million) and TOT ($10.2 million) funds but adds flexibility for loan repayments and land. The funds are described in the City's FY 2017-18 and 2018-19 adopted budget (source_url, Successor Agency and Housing Authority sections) and the Prohousing matrix; the current biennial budget PDF was not opened this pass, so balances are unconfirmed. State prevailing wage applies to housing successor funds.

record.program_name: American Canyon Affordable Housing Nexus Fee (ACMC 19.28.090) and Affordable Housing In-Lieu Fee Fund (Fund 340)
record.administering_agency: City of American Canyon Community Development Department and Finance Department
record.typical_award_size: Requirement, not a subsidy. 2026 fee per gross square foot (Resolution 2025-94, adopted December 2, 2025, effective January 31, 2026, CPI adjusted each year, capped at 2% under Resolution 2016-15): single family and townhouse $3.64, stacked flats and apartments $4.22, ADU $0.00, office, hotel, retail and other nonresidential $0.93, warehouse and industrial $0.60. Fund 340 unaudited balance at June 30, 2023 was $400,075 after FY 2022-23 collections of $217,698 and a $70,492 transfer for the 189 Theresa demolition; the FY 2024-25 AB 1600 report was accepted December 16, 2025 but could not be opened this pass.
record.affordability_requirement: ADUs and affordable housing (deed restricted to lower income households) are exempt. Fee revenue is restricted to housing affordable to very low and low income households.
record.next_deadline: Paid at building permit issuance. Next CPI adjustment resolution expected on a December 2026 Council consent agenda for January 2027 effectiveness.
record.layering_notes: The fund is small and the City spends it on services (landlord tenant assistance, Section 8 support, farmworker housing contribution, maintenance of City owned housing, rent stabilization administration) rather than development loans, so there is no American Canyon trust fund NOFA to layer; a developer asking for a City contribution should request a Council action on a case by case basis. Exemption of affordable projects means 100% affordable deals pay no City housing fee. Fee resolution read on the City's Legistar download host (source_url); code sections and the AB 1600 FY 2022-23 report (americancanyon.gov PDF, retrieved via WebFetch because the site blocks scripts) were also opened. Fee revenue sits on top of the Pass 2 County fee structure only for unincorporated parcels; inside city limits only the City fee applies.

record.program_name: St. Helena Affordable Housing Trust Fund (Fund 751, SHMC 17.30.050) development loans and project commitments
record.administering_agency: City of St. Helena Community Development Department and Administrative Services Director (fund administrator); City Council approves commitments
record.typical_award_size: Fund 751 beginning balance July 1, 2025 of $2,404,218, projected $2,448,125 at June 30, 2026 and $2,492,032 at June 30, 2027 before new commitments; recurring revenue is small (about $60,000 to $65,000 a year of housing impact and in-lieu fees plus interest, with a $583,991 spike in FY 2023-24). Track record: about $2,450,000 committed to Turley Flats (8 units, $700,000 incl. deferred fees), Brenkle Court (8 units) and 963 Pope Street (5 units) through 2021, and the Housing Element states the City has funded every developer request since 2015. Press reports (not confirmed on the City site) describe a $1.4 million loan to Our Town St. Helena for the Christine Apartments and a March 2026 commitment of $2.2 million ($1.5 million early, $700,000 later) to the 40 unit Fountain Street project by Our Town St. Helena and Burbank Housing (about $27 million total cost, land donated).
record.per_unit_cap: None published; recent commitments equal roughly $55,000 to $90,000 per unit.
record.affordability_requirement: Fund must be used solely to increase and improve housing affordable to moderate, low and very low income households, with priority for extremely low income households and the western part of the city (Programs H-DD and H-MM). Rental affordability agreements recorded; the City targets 55-year terms on assisted rental projects.
record.next_deadline: No NOFA; developers request funds directly and the City Council acts by resolution (typically one to two actions a year). Remaining uncommitted balance after the Fountain Street pledge should be confirmed with Community Development (707-968-2740, Director Leza Mikhail). The biennial review of fees and inclusionary requirements under 17.30.050(B) is due in 2026.
record.layering_notes: Small but reliable: St. Helena has funded every request since 2015 and pairs trust fund loans with reduced or deferred City fees (Program H-CC) and Measure E money (separate record). Stack order for a St. Helena deal: CTCAC credits, HCD programs, County Affordable Housing Fund (the County funded Turley Flats $798,000 and 963 Pope $200,000, see Pass 2 record), then City trust fund and Measure E, with HACN project based vouchers. City loans are public funds, so prevailing wage applies. Figures from the adopted FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 budget (source_url, Fund 751 worksheet); the 2023-2031 Housing Element draft on hcd.ca.gov and the code mirror were also opened. The City AgendaCenter search returned no results to scripts, so 2026 council actions rest on press coverage and are marked as such.

record.program_name: St. Helena Measure E 1% Transient Occupancy Tax for affordable and workforce housing (Fund 752)
record.administering_agency: City of St. Helena Administrative Services and Community Development Departments; City Council
record.typical_award_size: Special tax of 1% on hotel stays (TOT 12% to 13%) effective January 1, 2019, restricted to programs and services for affordable and workforce housing. Revenue about $300,000 to $315,000 a year (FY 2024-25 estimate $287,718 including interest; FY 2025-26 budget $322,504; FY 2026-27 $328,684). Fund balance $636,312 at July 1, 2025, projected $858,816 at June 30, 2026 and $1,187,500 at June 30, 2027 (includes a $160,000 long term receivable for an affordable housing loan). Only $100,000 of Planning and Building services is budgeted against it in FY 2026-27, so most of the balance is available for projects.
record.affordability_requirement: Households earning up to 120% AMI (rental and for sale), per the fund description; the City prioritizes extremely low and very low income units in its Housing Element programs.
record.next_deadline: No NOFA; City Council allocates by resolution. Press coverage indicates Measure E money is part of the two fund total (about $1.5 million) the Council pledged to Fountain Street in March 2026; confirm the uncommitted balance with the City.
record.layering_notes: Measure E is the City's only source for moderate income (81% to 120% AMI) units, which neither the trust fund's nexus based dollars nor state programs cover well; use it on workforce units in a mixed income project while the trust fund covers lower income units. Parallel to Napa's Measure F, Calistoga's Measure D and the County's Measure I, each a separate fund with its own geography. Figures from the adopted FY 2025-26 and 2026-27 budget (source_url, Fund 752 worksheet); the Housing Element estimate of $280,000 a year was also read.
